Finding a doctor on Medicare

People on Medicare and their families struggle to keep a doctor or find one who will take them.

“Without any notice from UHC, they cancelled our Primary Care Physician from their network effective 3/31/2026”, a member of a Medicare Advantage plan wrote on a forum in March 2026.

We read 53 public accounts from people on Medicare, their families and doctors' offices. More of the accounts from people and families were about losing a doctor, or not finding one who would take them, than about getting a wrong answer on whether a doctor is in their plan. CMS is building a national directory of doctors. Accurate listings in it could help people get the right answer. The directory could also say which kind of Medicare a practice takes new patients on. The first thing we would test is whether that saves people calls.

Where people look today

In these accounts, more people couldn't keep or find a doctor than got a wrong answer.

In 32 of the 42 accounts from people on Medicare or their families, the person could not keep a doctor or find one who would take them. In some, the doctor would not see them, did not take Medicare, or took other coverage but not theirs. In others, the doctor left their plan while they were in care, or the plan had no doctor nearby. In 9 accounts, the person got a wrong or conflicting answer about whether a doctor was in a plan. Five accounts had both problems.

In these accounts, people turned to a doctor's office or their insurance company more than anywhere else.

Some went without care. One woman could not afford out-of-network rates and stopped seeing her therapist. A retiree in Mississippi stopped going to the doctor.

When CMS checked Medicare Advantage directories between June 2022 and June 2024, it found that “44.29 percent of the location listings in the online provider directories contained at least one inaccuracy”. It gave that figure in its proposed rule of October 2026.

Losing a doctor

A doctor leaves someone's plan, or won't see them at all.

Some people were in care when a doctor, or a whole health system, left their Medicare Advantage plan. For others, the doctor took no new Medicare patients, or saw only people 65 or older. Some called office after office to find a doctor who would take them.

One. One called back
A man of 60 with a disability in Colorado, on the 31 doctors he contacted after his endocrinologist dropped him and other Medicare patients. He did find an endocrinologist in the end (2012).

What happened to them

Dropped from the network, no notice

A couple joined a Medicare Advantage plan on January 1, 2026. Their primary care doctor was dropped from its network as of March 31. They found out by logging into their account, less than two weeks before March 31. One of them wrote that March 31 was also the deadline for changing Medicare Advantage plans.

We received no notice of this change, but rather had to find out by going on line and logging into our account
A member, on an AARP forum (2026)

Rural, and stopped going

A retiree in Holly Springs, Mississippi, joined a Medicare Advantage plan. She found it did not cover the only health care provider within 25 miles of her home. She went back to Original Medicare with a supplement.

I didn't go to the doctor because I was going to have to pay out-of-pocket money I didn't have.
Told to NBC News (2023)

Under 65, on disability

A person under 65 was on Medicare through disability. Their primary care doctor chose to see only people 65 or older.

I cannot see specialists I need without a primary care's referral!
A person in New Mexico, on a forum (2022)

Turning 65

A woman turning 65 had seen the same therapist, a licensed marriage and family therapist, for about six years. Medicare did not pay those therapists until January 2024. She spent six months on a waiting list to see a social worker who took Medicare.

About six months before I turned 65, she told me that she was not going to be able to see me anymore because of the fact that I was going to be on Medicare.
A woman whose job is helping seniors find mental health services, on NPR (2024)

The man of 60, in Aurora, Colorado, got a letter from his endocrinologist saying he and the doctor's other Medicare patients were being dropped. When a woman in Washington, D.C., turned 65, her internist didn't take Medicare patients. It took her 18 months to find a new doctor. A forum poster believed their office was dropping them “because they don't want to take my Medicare anymore.” In Vancouver, Washington, a large clinic chain took Medicare Advantage plans but not people on Original Medicare, except to see a specialist. A reader replying in the comments gave a reason: such groups are in “a financial risk-sharing arrangement with Medicare Advantage plans.” In these four accounts, the person knew the doctor would not take them. None of them got a wrong answer.

Joan · new to Medicare

Joan's plan lists her doctor, but the doctor's office says the practice is not in her network.

Joan is a composite. Her age, the year, her start date and where she enrolled are made up. The other steps happened to real people who joined a Medicare Advantage plan because their doctor was listed.

I joined Medicare Advantage when I became eligible for Medicare a few months ago because my doctor was listed as a participating provider.
A reader's letter to AARP Bulletin's Medicare column (2026)

From the accounts

When we started, my primary care provider was listed so I went ahead and applied. I got a confirmation letter.
Someone choosing a plan with their wife, on an AARP forum (2020)

From the accounts

The day my coverage began, I attempted to make an appointment with the physician, but was told by the insurance billing office that none of the physicians in their office is in the network!
A reader's letter to PBS NewsHour (2017)

From the accounts

I spoke with a customer service representative from the MA plan and explained the inaccurate, discrepant information in its online directory.
The same reader (2017)

From a news story

CMS gives most Advantage members two chances to change plans: during the annual open enrollment period in the fall and from January until March 31.
KFF Health News (2024)

From CMS

This SEP is only open to people who relied on incorrect information from Plan Finder (not from a plan website).
CMS fact sheet, March 2026. SEP is short for special election period.

Joan turns 65 in spring 2026. She finds her doctor in an insurance company's online directory and enrolls in its Medicare Advantage plan on the company's website. Her Medicare and her plan both start on April 1.

On April 1 she calls her doctor's office to book a visit. The billing office tells her the practice is not in her plan's network.

She calls the insurance company and explains that its online directory is wrong.

She looks for a way to change plans. Most members get two chances a year, in the fall and from January to March 31. Neither is open in April.

For 2026, CMS opened a special election period for people who relied on wrong information in Plan Finder. Joan enrolled on the insurance company's website, so she does not qualify. If she had enrolled through Plan Finder and it had listed her doctor wrongly, she could have called 1-800-MEDICARE within her first 3 months on the plan.

Joan writes to an advice column to ask whether she can switch plans. A reader whose listed doctor was out of network asked PBS NewsHour the same thing in 2017. Another asked AARP Bulletin in 2026.

Under CMS's rules, Joan can change plans once, until the end of her third month on Medicare. Because she joined at 65, she can also switch to Original Medicare at any time in her first 12 months on the plan. The counselor who answered the AARP letter did not mention either option. Neither letter says enough to know whether those options applied, or what happened next.

Elena · caring for her father

Elena gets different answers on whether her father's specialist is in his network.

Elena is a composite too. Her father is on a Medicare Advantage plan, and she handles his care. Her name, and that she is a daughter, are made up. In the 2026 account, a son made the calls for his mother. The steps she takes happened to real families with Medicare Advantage plans, in accounts from 2015 and 2026.

From the accounts

He still thinks he has Medicare primary and UnitedHealthcare as a secondary insurance.
An adult child writing about their father, in Physicians Practice (2015)

From the accounts

A physician listed as in-network one day was listed as out-of-network the next.
Families USA, on a son's calls to his mother's insurance company (2026)

From the accounts

At check-in, the registration desk informed them the visit would be billed as out-of-network.
Families USA, on the same son and his mother (2026)

From the accounts

if there isn't a physician that fits the requirements of Dad's care, they would have to provide the authorization to see an out-of-network physician, as that was not Dad's problem they didn't fill up their network.
The adult child, on a call with their father's medical group (2015)

From the accounts

A few hours later poof! They found a doctor only 10 minutes from his house that was just credentialed that day.
The same adult child (2015)

Elena's father thinks he has Medicare with secondary insurance. He is on a Medicare Advantage plan. To see a specialist, he needs a referral from his primary care doctor.

His doctor refers him to a specialist. Elena calls his insurance company to check that the specialist is in its network. She gets different answers on different calls.

On one call the company says yes, so she drives him an hour and a half to the appointment. At check-in, the desk says the visit will be billed as out of network. When she tries to book the scan the specialist orders, she is told it is out of network too, at about $3,000.

She gets her father and his medical group on one call. If the group has no specialist he can see, she says, it has to authorize one outside the network.

A few hours later the group finds a specialist 10 minutes from his house, credentialed that day.

In the 2026 account, the son made calls for months. His mother started treatment seven months after he first took her to the emergency room. Families USA's account calls it “many failures, across many systems, over many years”. The adult child in the 2015 account, who works in medical billing, wrote about their father:

there is no way he would ever have been able to get this figured out without my help.
The adult child, on their father (2015)

Doctors' offices

Offices send the same details to every plan they work with, in the format that plan asks for.

Insurance companies list doctors partly from what offices send them. Dr. Jack Resneck Jr., president of the American Medical Association, spoke to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2023. He said practices typically contract with 20 or more plans and send every one a roster of their doctors. At the academic medical center where he works, he said, plans typically take 6 to 8 months to add or remove a doctor after the center tells them.

Two of the 11 accounts from doctors' offices are about Medicare Advantage plans. The rest are about insurance plans in general. None of the 11 is from a front-desk worker.

They do not use standardized formats, so we have to send different rosters with different formatting to each and every one.
Dr. Jack Resneck Jr., to the Senate Finance Committee (2023)

From the offices

17 forms, every 90 days

A social worker who runs a group practice in California has 17 insurance contracts. After a state law on directories passed, her insurance companies began sending her a form every 90 days to confirm her listing. Filling out all 17 takes about a day, unpaid.

I have 17 insurance contracts. I have to fill out 17 attestations
Told to the California Health Report (2021). An attestation is a form confirming a listing.

Listed as the wrong kind of doctor

A neurologist in a one-doctor office is listed as a psychiatrist. No insurance company has asked him to check his listing.

No, I'm not a psychiatrist. And no one's asked me.
In Texas Medicine (2023)

What one doctor would rather have

Patients told one Texas practice that a plan had dropped it from its directory. The insurance company could not say why. The practice's doctor would rather get an email from insurance companies, with a link to log in and check.

In an ideal world, I would say it's an email
In Texas Medicine (2023)

The National Provider Directory

CMS is building a national directory of doctors. A record in it shows a doctor's Medicare status.

CMS calls the National Provider Directory “a centralized, standardized repository intended to serve as the authoritative public-facing platform for provider directory information across the entire health tech ecosystem”. On November 20, 2026, it was a preview site at directory.cms.gov. Its help pages say it suits people who need detailed provider data. They send people on Medicare to Care Compare.

The record of a family doctor in Kansas, saved on November 20, 2026, showed Medicare as “Participating”. It listed Medicare as the only insurance and named no Medicare Advantage plan. One insurance company can sell many Medicare Advantage plans, and a doctor can be in some and not others. The record did not show whether the doctor was in any plan's network, which was Joan's question.

On Medicare.gov, Plan Finder shows which doctors are in a plan's network. For 2026, CMS bought Plan Finder's doctor lists from a vendor, as a short-term step. CMS warns that “some provider directory information may be incorrect, especially in this first year”. For 2027 plans, the insurance companies were scheduled to send the lists instead, from October 1, 2026. CMS says Plan Finder will later draw on the national directory.

Once insurance companies report their networks to the national directory, accurate listings could help people get the right answer about whether a doctor is in their plan. It cannot make a doctor take someone, or keep a network from changing. It could say which kind of Medicare a practice takes new patients on. The Kansas doctor's record answers “Accepting new patients” with a plain “Yes.” The American Medical Association warned senators that “a bloated provider directory may be hiding a network that is wholly inadequate to serve the needs of the plan's enrollees”.

The National Provider Directory (NPD) is in preview release.

What we would test first

We would start with five questions, and test them with people on Medicare, their families, counselors and doctors' offices.

  1. Would people make fewer calls if a directory showed which kind of Medicare a practice takes new patients on?

    Test with people on Original Medicare and on Medicare Advantage plans who are looking for a doctor, and with office managers at one-doctor offices and large groups.

  2. When a doctor or health system leaves a plan, how and when do people find out? What do they believe they can do?

    Test with people on Medicare Advantage plans in the middle of care with a doctor, SHIP counselors, and family members who make the calls.

  3. Before joining a plan, how do people check that their doctors are in it? What do they take as the answer?

    Test with people choosing or changing a Medicare Advantage plan, including people new to Medicare, and family members who make the calls.

  4. When a record says a doctor participates in Medicare, do people on a Medicare Advantage plan think the doctor is in their plan?

    Test with people on Medicare Advantage plans and on Original Medicare, side by side.

  5. How would an office like to check and correct its listing?

    A form from every plan, a fax, an email with a link, or a doctor signing in to the directory. Test with doctors, practice owners and front-desk staff, from one-doctor offices to large centers.

I'm sticking with her because she knows everything about me
A woman in Durham, North Carolina, on her doctor. A SHIP counselor helped her change plans before the December 7 enrollment deadline, so she could keep the doctor (2023).

Prepared by Focus Consulting, November 2026. The storybook draws on 53 public accounts dated 2008 to 2026. Forty-two are from people on Medicare or family helping them, and 11 are from doctors' offices. AI helped find them in forums, news stories, hearing records and advocacy pages, and every one was saved before use. A script confirmed that every quote on this page appears word for word in its saved source.

An AI model tagged all 451 quotes with problems from a fixed list. It found 32 accounts about a doctor people can't keep or find, and 9 about a wrong answer. A second model, working without the first one's results, found 30 and 8. A researcher then checked 5 of the tags behind the counts, drawn at random. Four held up. The fifth was moved from the wrong-answer count to the can't-keep-or-find count.

Joan and Elena are composites. Their names and some details are made up. The steps they go through come from real, cited accounts. Private people are described by their role, not their name. The sources are listed on a separate page.
